statement: Security requirements for user endpoint devices, such as registration, encryption, screen lock, patching, anti-malware and remote wipe, are set and extended to personally owned devices where those are allowed. Device management tools check devices against the requirements continuously, and non-compliant devices are fixed or cut off from company data. This keeps lost, stolen or poorly maintained devices from exposing company data. Proof is the endpoint policy and the device compliance report.
why_asked: A policy that nobody checks leaves unencrypted, unpatched or unmanaged laptops and phones holding company data. Consultants need to see that devices are measured against the rules, not just that rules exist.
how_to_ask: Ask what the device rules are, whether personal devices are allowed, and how the organization knows a given device meets the rules today. Ask to see a live compliance view, not a screenshot of the policy. Example probe: "Show me how many managed devices are currently out of compliance, and what happens to them."
question: Does your organization make sure user endpoint devices meet its security requirements?
expected_evidence: Endpoint device and personal device policy; device management compliance report; list of exceptions with approvals; remote wipe or device removal records. Cover the last audit period.
good_looks_like: A written endpoint policy states the minimum settings and says whether personal devices are allowed. A device management or endpoint tool reports compliance for all in-scope devices, with exceptions approved and non-compliant devices followed up. Results are reviewed and followed up.
test: Read the endpoint policy and confirm it sets minimum settings, including for personal devices if allowed. Pull the current device compliance report and sample devices from it. Pass if the sampled devices meet the required settings (for example disk encryption on, supported operating system) or have an approved exception.
baseline_risk: Lost, stolen or unmanaged devices expose company data and become an easy way into the network.

statement: A secure configuration baseline is documented for each type of operating system, database, cloud account and network device in scope. Compliance scans or configuration monitoring compare live systems with the baselines, and drift is fixed. Each baseline is reviewed on its own defined cycle, and the version history shows it. This reduces weaknesses from default or drifting settings.
why_asked: Systems built from defaults or left to drift carry avoidable weaknesses that attackers and scanners find first. Consultants test whether baselines exist, are checked against live systems and are kept current.
how_to_ask: Ask which technology types have a baseline, how systems are checked against it, and when each baseline was last reviewed. Example probe: "Pick a production database server and show me its baseline, its last compliance scan and any drift that was fixed."
question: Does your organization maintain secure configuration baselines and check systems against them?
expected_evidence: Configuration baselines per technology type with version history; compliance scan or configuration monitoring reports; drift remediation tickets; hardening standard. Cover the last two review cycles.
good_looks_like: Baselines exist for every in-scope technology type and are version controlled. Scans or cloud posture tools run on a defined cycle, drift is ticketed and fixed, and each baseline shows a review within its stated interval.
test: List the in-scope technology types and confirm each has a baseline. Sample systems and check the latest compliance scan results against the baseline, then trace drift findings to fixes. Pass if every type has a baseline, sampled systems are scanned, drift is remediated, and each baseline was reviewed within its stated interval.
baseline_risk: Systems run with default or inconsistent settings that leave known weaknesses open to attack.

statement: A network security standard is set and maintained, covering how networks and network devices are secured and managed, including device hardening, administrator access and encryption in transit. A current network diagram of the in-scope environment is kept, including cloud networks and links to third parties. Firewall and security group rules are reviewed on a defined cycle, and unneeded or overly permissive rules are removed. This limits the paths an attacker can use. Proof is the standard, the diagram and the rule review records.
why_asked: Stale diagrams and unreviewed firewall rules hide exposed services and old access paths. Consultants use the diagram and the rule review records to see whether the network is understood and controlled.
how_to_ask: Ask for the diagram and check its date, then ask who reviews firewall rules and what they removed last time. Example probe: "Walk me through your last firewall rule review and name one rule you removed."
question: Does your organization keep its networks secured, documented and regularly reviewed?
expected_evidence: Network security standard; current network diagram including cloud and third-party connections; firewall and security group rule review records with removals; change tickets for rule removals. Cover the last two review cycles.
good_looks_like: A network standard defines secure management of devices and traffic. The diagram matches reality, including cloud and partner links. Rule reviews are recorded, and unneeded or permissive rules lead to documented changes.
test: Check the diagram's last update date and compare it with a sample of live network components or cloud networks. Inspect the latest firewall and security group review record and trace sampled removals to change tickets. Pass if the diagram is current and complete, the standard exists, and a review happened in the period with permissive rules removed.
baseline_risk: Unknown or overly permissive network paths let attackers move or reach systems that should be unreachable.

statement: The security features, service levels and requirements of each network service the organization uses, such as internet links, DNS, VPN, content delivery and managed connectivity, are documented. Where a provider supplies the service, these terms are written into the agreement. Service reports are reviewed against the agreed levels on a defined cycle. This keeps the organization from depending on network services that do not meet its needs. Proof is the service agreements and the review records.
why_asked: Network services supplied by others often carry security and availability promises nobody checks. Consultants look for whether the terms are written down and measured.
how_to_ask: Ask for a list of network services and who provides each one, then ask how performance and security are tracked. Example probe: "Show me the last service report for your main internet or VPN provider and who reviewed it."
question: Does your organization document and monitor the security of the network services it uses?
expected_evidence: List of network services and providers; service agreements stating security features and service levels; service level reports with review sign-off. Cover the last two review cycles.
good_looks_like: Every network service has its security features, service levels and requirements documented, and provider-supplied ones are covered by contract. Service reports are reviewed against the agreed levels and shortfalls are raised with the provider.
test: List the network services in use and sample some of them. For each, check the documented requirements and the latest service level report. Pass if requirements are documented, external ones are in contracts, and reports were reviewed against the agreed levels in the period.
baseline_risk: Weak or unmeasured network services cause outages and exposure the organization only discovers after the fact.

statement: Network segments are defined by trust level or function, such as production, development, corporate, guest and management, and the traffic allowed between them is stated. The design is enforced through firewall, VLAN or security group settings. Configuration exports show the enforcement. This limits how far an intruder can move from one compromised system.
why_asked: A flat network lets one compromised machine reach everything. Consultants need proof that the segmentation design is actually enforced in configuration.
how_to_ask: Ask for the segmentation design, then ask to see the firewall or security group rules that enforce one boundary. Example probe: "Show me what stops the guest network from reaching production, in the actual rules."
question: Does your organization separate its networks into segments by trust level and enforce the allowed traffic between them?
expected_evidence: Segmentation standard and network diagram showing segments and allowed flows; firewall, VLAN or security group configuration export for sampled segments. Cover the current configuration and the last change review.
good_looks_like: Segments and permitted flows are documented, and exports of firewall, VLAN or cloud rules match the design. Changes to boundaries go through change control.
test: Pick sample segment boundaries from the design, such as guest to production and development to production. Inspect the configuration export for each. Pass if the configured rules enforce the documented allowed traffic and block the rest.
baseline_risk: An intruder who reaches one system can move freely to critical systems and data.

statement: The categories of external website that are blocked, and how exceptions are approved, are set in a policy. A filtering control such as a secure web gateway, DNS filtering or an endpoint agent enforces the policy for all in-scope users, including remote users. This reduces exposure to malicious content. Proof is the policy and the filtering configuration or report.
why_asked: Users who browse freely, especially off the office network, are an easy route for malware and phishing. Consultants check that filtering follows people wherever they work.
how_to_ask: Ask which categories are blocked, how exceptions are approved and whether the filter works on laptops outside the office. Example probe: "If I am at home on a company laptop, what stops me from opening a known malware site?"
question: Does your organization control access to external websites for all users, including remote users?
expected_evidence: Web access policy listing blocked categories and exception process; filtering configuration export; filtering activity or block report; remote user coverage statement. Cover the last audit period.
good_looks_like: A policy defines blocked categories and an exception route. A filtering tool is active for office and remote users, and activity reports show blocks occurring.
test: Read the policy and the filtering configuration. Sample users, including remote ones, and confirm the filter applies to them, and check that a blocked category test URL is refused. Pass if filtering is active for the sampled users and matches the policy.
baseline_risk: Users reach malicious sites unchecked, raising the chance of malware infection and credential theft.

statement: The approved reference time sources for in-scope systems are named in a standard. Systems are configured to synchronize with those sources through network time settings or the cloud provider's time service. Configuration exports show the setting. This keeps log timestamps consistent so events can be reconstructed across systems.
why_asked: Unsynchronized clocks make it impossible to line up logs during an investigation. Consultants spot-check the setting instead of reading the standard alone.
how_to_ask: Ask which time sources are approved and how systems are pointed at them. Example probe: "Show me the time settings on one server, one network device and one cloud workload."
question: Does your organization synchronize the clocks of its systems to approved time sources?
expected_evidence: Standard naming approved time sources; system configuration exports showing time settings for sampled systems; baseline configuration that includes time. Cover the current configuration.
good_looks_like: A standard names the approved sources, and baselines or configuration management push the setting to all system types. Sampled systems all point at the approved sources.
test: Read the standard for the named sources. Sample servers, network devices and cloud workloads and inspect their time settings. Pass if every sampled system synchronizes with an approved source.
baseline_risk: Mismatched clocks make logs unreliable for investigations and weaken evidence of what happened.

statement: Rules state who may install software on operational systems, from which approved sources and with what testing and approval. Technical restrictions enforce this on servers and endpoints, for example no local administrator rights, application allow lists or deployment only through the pipeline. This stops unauthorized or untested software from reaching production. Proof is the procedure and the configuration or policy exports.
why_asked: Unrestricted installs let malware, unlicensed tools and untested code onto operational systems. Consultants check that the restriction is technical, not just a rule.
how_to_ask: Ask who can install software and how that is enforced on both servers and laptops. Example probe: "If a developer tried to install an unapproved tool on a production server, what would stop them?"
question: Does your organization restrict and technically enforce who can install software on its operational systems?
expected_evidence: Software installation procedure with approved sources and approval steps; endpoint or server policy export showing administrator rights or allow list settings; deployment pipeline records. Cover the last audit period.
good_looks_like: A procedure states who may install what, from where, with what approval. Technical controls such as removed local admin rights or allow lists enforce it on servers and endpoints, and exceptions are approved and recorded.
test: Read the procedure. Sample servers and endpoints and inspect their policy exports for installation restrictions. Pass if the sampled systems block unapproved installs and any exception has an approval record.
baseline_risk: Unauthorized or untested software enters operational systems and introduces malware or instability.

statement: Security requirements for working outside company premises, such as approved devices, secure connections, physical privacy and handling of printed material, are set. Technical controls enforce them for remote access, for example a VPN or zero trust gateway with multi-factor sign-in and device compliance checks. This protects company data when people work from home or travel. Proof is the remote working policy and the access gateway configuration.
why_asked: Remote workers sit outside the office defenses, so the rules must be enforced at the access point. Consultants look for both a written rule and a technical gate.
how_to_ask: Ask what remote workers must follow and what stops a non-compliant device or user from connecting. Example probe: "Show me what happens when a remote user connects from an unmanaged laptop."
question: Does your organization enforce security requirements for remote working through technical controls on remote access?
expected_evidence: Remote working policy; remote access gateway or VPN configuration; multi-factor and device compliance settings; sample access logs showing denied non-compliant attempts. Cover the last audit period.
good_looks_like: A remote working policy covers devices, connections, privacy and printed material. Remote access requires strong authentication and compliant devices, and logs show the rules being applied.
test: Read the policy for the required topics. Inspect the remote access configuration and test or review logs for sampled users and devices. Pass if remote access requires multi-factor sign-in and device checks as the policy states.
baseline_risk: Remote access paths become an easy entry point for attackers and expose data outside company control.
